Chapter 15 · Modules 15-1 to 15-6 · 16–23 Nov

Oscillations

15-1Simple harmonic motion

Class 30 · Mon 16 Nov

  • Period and frequency. One oscillation takes the period TTT; the frequency f=1Tf=\frac{1}{T}f=T1​ counts oscillations per second, in hertz (1 Hz=1 s−11\text{ Hz}=1\text{ s}^{-1}1 Hz=1 s−1).
  • Simple harmonic motion (SHM) is a displacement that goes as a cosine, with amplitude xmx_mxm​, angular frequency ω\omegaω (rad/s) and phase constant ϕ\phiϕ: x(t)=xmcos⁡(ωt+ϕ),ω=2πT=2πfx(t)=x_m\cos(\omega t+\phi),\qquad \omega=\frac{2\pi}{T}=2\pi fx(t)=xm​cos(ωt+ϕ),ω=T2π​=2πf
  • Velocity and acceleration come from differentiating: v=−ωxmsin⁡(ωt+ϕ)v=-\omega x_m\sin(\omega t+\phi)v=−ωxm​sin(ωt+ϕ) and a=−ω2xmcos⁡(ωt+ϕ),a=-\omega^2x_m\cos(\omega t+\phi),a=−ω2xm​cos(ωt+ϕ), so a=−ω2xa=-\omega^2xa=−ω2x
  • Where the extremes are. The speed is largest, ωxm\omega x_mωxm​, at x=0x=0x=0; the acceleration is largest, ω2xm\omega^2x_mω2xm​, at the turning points x=±xmx=\pm x_mx=±xm​.
  • The force law. A restoring force proportional to the displacement, F=−kxF=-kxF=−kx, gives SHM. For a block on a spring ω=km,T=2πmk\omega=\sqrt{\frac{k}{m}},\qquad T=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{m}{k}}ω=mk​​,T=2πkm​​ The period doesn't depend on the amplitude.
Worked example15-1

A 0.500.500.50 kg block on a frictionless floor is fixed to a spring with k=50k=50k=50 N/m. It is pulled 0.200.200.20 m from equilibrium and released from rest at t=0t=0t=0.

  1. (a)Find the angular frequency, the period and the frequency.
  2. (b)Write x(t)x(t)x(t).
  3. (c)Find the greatest speed and the greatest acceleration.
  4. (d)How fast is the block moving as it passes x=0.12x=0.12x=0.12 m?

15-2Energy in simple harmonic motion

Class 31 · Tue 17 Nov

  • Two kinds of energy: the spring's potential energy and the block's kinetic energy, U=12kx2,K=12mv2U=\tfrac{1}{2}kx^2,\qquad K=\tfrac{1}{2}mv^2U=21​kx2,K=21​mv2
  • Mechanical energy is conserved without friction. It is all potential at the turning points and all kinetic at x=0x=0x=0: E=U+K=12kxm2=12mvm2E=U+K=\tfrac{1}{2}kx_m^2=\tfrac{1}{2}mv_m^2E=U+K=21​kxm2​=21​mvm2​
  • Speed at any position. From 12mv2=12k(xm2−x2)\frac{1}{2}mv^2=\frac{1}{2}k(x_m^2-x^2)21​mv2=21​k(xm2​−x2): v=ωxm2−x2v=\omega\sqrt{x_m^2-x^2}v=ωxm2​−x2​
  • How the energy is shared. At x=xm2x=\frac{x_m}{2}x=2xm​​ only a quarter of it is potential; U=KU=KU=K at x=±xm2.x=\pm\frac{x_m}{\sqrt2}.x=±2​xm​​.
Worked example15-2

A 2.02.02.0 kg block on a spring with k=200k=200k=200 N/m oscillates on a frictionless floor with an amplitude of 0.100.100.10 m.

  2. (b)Find the greatest speed.
  3. (c)Find the potential energy, the kinetic energy and the speed at x=0.060x=0.060x=0.060 m.
  4. (d)Where is the kinetic energy equal to the potential energy?

15-3An angular simple harmonic oscillator

Not on the class scheduleThe schedule doesn’t list it; it may come up in a class marked TBD.

  • A torsion pendulum is a disk hung on a wire. Twisted by an angle θ\thetaθ, the wire twists back with a torque proportional to the angle (κ\kappaκ, the torsion constant, in N·m/rad): τ=−κθ\tau=-\kappa\thetaτ=−κθ
  • Angular SHM. It is a block on a spring with m→Im\to Im→I and k→κk\to\kappak→κ: θ=θmcos⁡(ωt+ϕ)\theta=\theta_m\cos(\omega t+\phi)θ=θm​cos(ωt+ϕ) with ω=κI,T=2πIκ\omega=\sqrt{\frac{\kappa}{I}},\qquad T=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{I}{\kappa}}ω=Iκ​​,T=2πκI​​
  • Measuring rotational inertia. On the same wire T∝IT\propto\sqrt{I}T∝I​, so I2I1=(T2T1)2.\frac{I_2}{I_1}=\left(\frac{T_2}{T_1}\right)^2.I1​I2​​=(T1​T2​​)2.

15-4Pendulums, circular motion

Class 32 · Thu 19 Nov

  • The simple pendulum. A small bob on a string of length LLL. The restoring torque is −mgLsin⁡θ≈−mgLθ-mgL\sin\theta\approx-mgL\theta−mgLsinθ≈−mgLθ for small angles (θ\thetaθ in radians), which is SHM with T=2πLgT=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{L}{g}}T=2πgL​​ Neither the mass nor a small amplitude changes the period.
  • The physical pendulum. A rigid body swinging about a pivot a distance hhh from its centre of mass: T=2πImghT=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{I}{mgh}}T=2πmghI​​ A simple pendulum has I=mL2I=mL^2I=mL2 and h=Lh=Lh=L, which gives the formula above.
  • SHM and circular motion. A point going round a circle of radius xmx_mxm​ at a steady angular speed ω\omegaω has x=xmcos⁡(ωt+ϕ)x=x_m\cos(\omega t+\phi)x=xm​cos(ωt+ϕ): its shadow on a diameter moves in SHM.

15-5Damped simple harmonic motion

Class 33 · Fri 20 Nov

  • Damping. A drag force proportional to the velocity, Fd=−bvF_d=-bvFd​=−bv (bbb, the damping constant, in kg/s), makes the oscillation die away: x(t)=xme−bt/2mcos⁡(ω′t+ϕ)x(t)=x_me^{-bt/2m}\cos(\omega' t+\phi)x(t)=xm​e−bt/2mcos(ω′t+ϕ)
  • The damped angular frequency ω′=km−b24m2\omega'=\sqrt{\frac{k}{m}-\frac{b^2}{4m^2}}ω′=mk​−4m2b2​​ is almost ω\omegaω when the damping is small.
  • Energy. The amplitude falls as e−bt/2me^{-bt/2m}e−bt/2m, so the energy, which goes as the amplitude squared, falls twice as fast: E(t)≈12kxm2e−bt/mE(t)\approx\tfrac{1}{2}kx_m^2e^{-bt/m}E(t)≈21​kxm2​e−bt/m
  • Halving times. The amplitude halves in 2mbln⁡2\frac{2m}{b}\ln2b2m​ln2, the energy in mbln⁡2\frac{m}{b}\ln2bm​ln2.
Worked example15-5

A 0.250.250.25 kg block on a spring with k=100k=100k=100 N/m oscillates with a damping constant of 0.0500.0500.050 kg/s. Use ln⁡2≈0.69\ln2\approx0.69ln2≈0.69 and e−2≈0.14.e^{-2}\approx0.14.e−2≈0.14.

  1. (a)Find the angular frequency without damping and with it.
  2. (b)How long does the amplitude take to fall to half?
  3. (c)How long does the energy take to fall to half?
  4. (d)What fraction of the energy is left after 101010 s?

15-6Forced oscillations and resonance

Class 34 · Mon 23 Nov

  • Free and driven. Left alone, an oscillator swings at its natural angular frequency ω=km.\omega=\sqrt{\frac{k}{m}}.ω=mk​​. Pushed by a periodic force at ωd\omega_dωd​, it settles into oscillating at ωd\omega_dωd​.
  • Resonance. The amplitude is largest when the drive matches the natural frequency: ωd≈ω\omega_d\approx\omegaωd​≈ω
  • Damping lowers the resonance peak and widens it; with little damping the peak is tall and narrow.
  • Everyday resonance: pushing a swing once per swing, or an earthquake shaking a building at its natural frequency.
Worked example15-6

A 0.400.400.40 kg block on a spring with k=160k=160k=160 N/m, lightly damped, is driven by a force Fmcos⁡ωdtF_m\cos\omega_dtFm​cosωd​t.

  1. (a)At what driving angular frequency is the amplitude largest? Give the frequency in hertz too.
  2. (b)The drive is set to 2.02.02.0 Hz. At what frequency does the block oscillate once it has settled?
  3. (c)What mass, on the same spring, would resonate at 2.02.02.0 Hz?
Show solutionHide solution

Watch out

  • Using degrees in ωt+ϕ\omega t+\phiωt+ϕ: the phase is in radians, and so is θ\thetaθ in sin⁡θ≈θ.\sin\theta\approx\theta.sinθ≈θ.
  • Mixing up ω\omegaω (rad/s) and fff (Hz): ω=2πf\omega=2\pi fω=2πf.
  • Putting the greatest speed at the turning points: it is at the centre, where the acceleration is zero.
  • The spring's period depends on the mass; the simple pendulum's doesn't. Neither depends on the amplitude.
  • With damping the amplitude goes as e−bt/2me^{-bt/2m}e−bt/2m, but the energy as e−bt/me^{-bt/m}e−bt/m.

Waves I

16-1Transverse waves

Class 36 · Thu 26 Nov

  • Transverse and longitudinal. In a transverse wave (on a string) each element moves perpendicular to the wave's travel; in a longitudinal wave (sound) it moves along it.
  • A sinusoidal wave travelling toward +x+x+x: y(x,t)=ymsin⁡(kx−ωt)y(x,t)=y_m\sin(kx-\omega t)y(x,t)=ym​sin(kx−ωt) With kx+ωtkx+\omega tkx+ωt it travels toward −x-x−x.
  • Wave number and angular frequency: k=2πλk=\frac{2\pi}{\lambda}k=λ2π​ (rad/m) and ω=2πT=2πf.\omega=\frac{2\pi}{T}=2\pi f.ω=T2π​=2πf. A crest moves one wavelength each period: v=ωk=λT=λfv=\frac{\omega}{k}=\frac{\lambda}{T}=\lambda fv=kω​=Tλ​=λf
  • An element's own velocity u=∂y∂t=−ωymcos⁡(kx−ωt)u=\frac{\partial y}{\partial t}=-\omega y_m\cos(kx-\omega t)u=∂t∂y​=−ωym​cos(kx−ωt) is across the string, up to ωym\omega y_mωym​. It is not the wave speed vvv.

A wave on a string is y=0.020sin⁡(4.0πx−20πt),y=0.020\sin(4.0\pi x-20\pi t),y=0.020sin(4.0πx−20πt), with xxx and yyy in metres and ttt in seconds.

  1. (a)Find the amplitude and the wavelength.
  2. (b)Find the frequency and the period.

  4. (d)Find the greatest transverse speed of an element of the string.

16-2Wave speed on a stretched string

Class 37 · Fri 27 Nov

  • Speed on a string. It is set by the tension τ\tauτ and the linear density μ=mL\mu=\frac{m}{L}μ=Lm​ (kg/m): v=τμv=\sqrt{\frac{\tau}{\mu}}v=μτ​​
  • The string sets the speed; the source sets the frequency. On one string a higher frequency means a shorter wavelength, λ=vf,\lambda=\frac{v}{f},λ=fv​, at the same speed.
  • Into another string the frequency stays the same, while the speed and the wavelength change together.
Worked example16-2

A string 2.02.02.0 m long with a mass of 101010 g is stretched with a tension of 505050 N.

  2. (b)Find the wave speed.

16-3Energy and power of a wave traveling along a string

Class 37 · Fri 27 Nov

  • Energy on the move. Each element has kinetic energy (it moves up and down) and elastic potential energy (it is stretched). Both are largest as it passes y=0y=0y=0 and zero at y=±ymy=\pm y_my=±ym​.
  • Average power carried by a sinusoidal wave on a string: Pavg=12μvω2ym2P_\text{avg}=\tfrac{1}{2}\mu v\omega^2y_m^2Pavg​=21​μvω2ym2​
  • Scaling. The power goes as the square of the amplitude and as the square of the frequency: doubling either makes it four times larger.
Worked example16-3

A sinusoidal wave runs along a string with μ=5.0×10−3\mu=5.0\times10^{-3}μ=5.0×10−3 kg/m and v=100v=100v=100 m/s. Its amplitude is 1.01.01.0 cm and its angular frequency 200200200 rad/s.

  1. (a)Find the average power it carries.
  2. (b)Find the power if the amplitude is doubled.

16-4The wave equation

Class 38 · Mon 30 Nov

  • The wave equation. Newton's second law for a short piece of string gives ∂2y∂x2=1v2∂2y∂t2\frac{\partial^2y}{\partial x^2}=\frac{1}{v^2}\frac{\partial^2y}{\partial t^2}∂x2∂2y​=v21​∂t2∂2y​ with v=τμ.v=\sqrt{\frac{\tau}{\mu}}.v=μτ​​.
  • Every travelling shape solves it. Any y=h(kx±ωt),y=h(kx\pm\omega t),y=h(kx±ωt), a shape moving without changing, satisfies it with v=ωk.v=\frac{\omega}{k}.v=kω​.
  • Reading off the speed: take both second derivatives of a solution; their ratio is v2v^2v2.

16-5Interference of waves

Class 40 · Thu 3 Dec

  • Superposition. Overlapping waves add, y′=y1+y2y'=y_1+y_2y′=y1​+y2​, and each passes through the other unchanged.
  • Two equal waves (same amplitude ymy_mym​, frequency and direction) with a phase difference ϕ\phiϕ make one wave: y′=[2ymcos⁡ϕ2]sin⁡(kx−ωt+ϕ2)y'=\left[2y_m\cos\tfrac{\phi}{2}\right]\sin\left(kx-\omega t+\tfrac{\phi}{2}\right)y′=[2ym​cos2ϕ​]sin(kx−ωt+2ϕ​)
  • Fully constructive for ϕ=0,2π,…\phi=0,2\pi,\dotsϕ=0,2π,… (amplitude 2ym2y_m2ym​); fully destructive for ϕ=π,3π,…\phi=\pi,3\pi,\dotsϕ=π,3π,… (amplitude 000).
  • Phase and wavelength. A shift of one wavelength is 2π2\pi2π rad: half a wavelength is π\piπ, a quarter π2\frac{\pi}{2}2π​.
Worked example16-5

16-6Phasors

Class 42 · Mon 7 Dec

  • A phasor is an arrow of length ymy_mym​ turning at angular speed ω\omegaω; its projection on the vertical axis is an element's displacement ymsin⁡ωty_m\sin\omega tym​sinωt.
  • Adding waves of the same frequency and direction, even with different amplitudes: add their phasors head to tail like vectors, the second turned by the phase difference ϕ\phiϕ.
  • The resultant amplitude follows from the law of cosines, (ym′)2=ym12+ym22+2ym1ym2cos⁡ϕ(y_m')^2=y_{m1}^2+y_{m2}^2+2y_{m1}y_{m2}\cos\phi(ym′​)2=ym12​+ym22​+2ym1​ym2​cosϕ and its phase β\betaβ is the direction of the summed arrow.
Worked example16-6

  2. (b)Find the resultant amplitude for phase differences of 000 and π\piπ rad.

16-7Standing waves and resonance

Class 41 · Fri 4 Dec

  • A standing wave. Two equal waves running in opposite directions add to y′=[2ymsin⁡kx]cos⁡ωty'=\left[2y_m\sin kx\right]\cos\omega ty′=[2ym​sinkx]cosωt Every element oscillates in place, with an amplitude that depends on xxx.
  • Nodes (which never move) are at x=0,λ2,λ,…x=0,\frac{\lambda}{2},\lambda,\dotsx=0,2λ​,λ,…; antinodes (amplitude 2ym2y_m2ym​) lie halfway between. Neighbouring nodes are λ2\frac{\lambda}{2}2λ​ apart.
  • A string fixed at both ends resonates when a whole number of half wavelengths fits, L=nλ2L=n\frac{\lambda}{2}L=n2λ​: fn=nv2L,n=1,2,3,…f_n=\frac{nv}{2L},\qquad n=1,2,3,\dotsfn​=2Lnv​,n=1,2,3,… The nnnth harmonic has nnn loops; n=1n=1n=1 is the fundamental.
Worked example16-7

A string 0.800.800.80 m long, fixed at both ends, has a tension of 727272 N and a linear density of 5.05.05.0 g/m.

  1. (a)Find the wave speed and the fundamental frequency.
  2. (b)Find the wavelength and frequency of the third harmonic, shown in the figure.
  3. (c)How many nodes does the third harmonic have, counting the ends?
  4. (d)What tension makes the fundamental 150150150 Hz?
Show solutionHide solution

Watch out

  • Mixing up the wave speed v=λfv=\lambda fv=λf, along the string, with an element's transverse speed uuu, across it.
  • On one string, a new frequency changes the wavelength, not the speed.
  • Forgetting the 2π2\pi2π: k=2πλk=\frac{2\pi}{\lambda}k=λ2π​ and ω=2πf\omega=2\pi fω=2πf.
  • Neighbouring nodes are half a wavelength apart, not a whole one.
  • The sign in kx±ωtkx\pm\omega tkx±ωt gives the direction: minus travels toward +x+x+x.

Chapter 17 · Modules 17-1 to 17-8 · 8–14 Dec

Waves II

17-1Speed of sound

Class 43 · Tue 8 Dec

  • Sound is longitudinal: elements of the medium oscillate along the direction the wave travels, squeezing and stretching it.
  • The speed depends on the medium's stiffness, its bulk modulus BBB, and on its density ρ\rhoρ: v=Bρ,B=−ΔpΔV/Vv=\sqrt{\frac{B}{\rho}},\qquad B=-\frac{\Delta p}{\Delta V/V}v=ρB​​,B=−ΔV/VΔp​
  • Typical speeds: about 343343343 m/s in air at 20 ∘20\ ^\circ20 ∘C, about 150015001500 m/s in water, several km/s in solids.
  • As on a string, the medium sets vvv and the source sets fff, so λ=vf.\lambda=\frac{v}{f}.λ=fv​.
Worked example17-1

Take the bulk modulus of water as 2.25×1092.25\times10^92.25×109 Pa, its density as 1000 kg/m3,1000\ \text{kg/m}^3,1000 kg/m3, and the speed of sound in air as 343343343 m/s.

  1. (a)Find the speed of sound in water.
  2. (b)Find the wavelength of a 3.003.003.00 kHz tone in water and in air.
  3. (c)Thunder arrives 3.03.03.0 s after a lightning flash. How far away is the storm?

17-2Traveling sound waves

Class 43 · Tue 8 Dec

  • The displacement wave. An element at xxx moves back and forth along xxx: s(x,t)=smcos⁡(kx−ωt)s(x,t)=s_m\cos(kx-\omega t)s(x,t)=sm​cos(kx−ωt)
  • The pressure wave. The pressure varies about its normal value by Δp(x,t)=Δpmsin⁡(kx−ωt)Δpm=vρωsm\begin{gathered}\Delta p(x,t)=\Delta p_m\sin(kx-\omega t)\\\Delta p_m=v\rho\omega s_m\end{gathered}Δp(x,t)=Δpm​sin(kx−ωt)Δpm​=vρωsm​​
  • A quarter cycle apart. Where the displacement is largest the pressure change is zero, and the other way round.
  • Tiny changes: even a very loud sound has a Δpm\Delta p_mΔpm​ of only tens of pascals, against 1.01×1051.01\times10^51.01×105 Pa of air pressure.

A sound wave in air has an angular frequency of 100010001000 rad/s and a displacement amplitude of 1.0×10−51.0\times10^{-5}1.0×10−5 m. Take v=340v=340v=340 m/s and ρ=1.20 kg/m3.\rho=1.20\ \text{kg/m}^3.ρ=1.20 kg/m3.

17-3Interference

Class 44 · Thu 10 Dec

  • Two sources in phase with the same wavelength: at a point, the waves arrive with a path length difference ΔL\Delta LΔL, which gives a phase difference ϕ=ΔLλ2π\phi=\frac{\Delta L}{\lambda}2\piϕ=λΔL​2π
  • Fully constructive when ΔL=0,λ,2λ,…,\Delta L=0,\lambda,2\lambda,\dots,ΔL=0,λ,2λ,…, a whole number of wavelengths.
  • Fully destructive when ΔL=λ2,3λ2,…,\Delta L=\frac{\lambda}{2},\frac{3\lambda}{2},\dots,ΔL=2λ​,23λ​,…, a whole number and a half.
  • In between, the interference is intermediate.

17-4Intensity and sound level

Class 44 · Thu 10 Dec

  • Intensity is power per area, I=PAI=\frac{P}{A}I=AP​, in W/m2\text{W/m}^2W/m2; for a sound wave I=12ρvω2sm2.I=\frac{1}{2}\rho v\omega^2s_m^2.I=21​ρvω2sm2​.
  • A point source spreading evenly in all directions: I=Ps4πr2I=\frac{P_s}{4\pi r^2}I=4πr2Ps​​ Twice as far, a quarter of the intensity.
  • Sound level in decibels, with the reference intensity I0=10−12 W/m2I_0=10^{-12}\ \text{W/m}^2I0​=10−12 W/m2: β=(10 dB)log⁡II0\beta=(10\ \text{dB})\log\frac{I}{I_0}β=(10 dB)logI0​I​
  • Rules of thumb: ten times the intensity adds 101010 dB, a hundred times adds 202020 dB, and twice adds about 333 dB (log⁡2≈0.30\log2\approx0.30log2≈0.30).

17-5Sources of musical sound

Class 45 · Fri 11 Dec

  • Standing sound waves in a pipe. An open end is (nearly) a displacement antinode; a closed end is a node.
  • Open at both ends: L=nλ2,L=n\frac{\lambda}{2},L=n2λ​, so f=nv2L,n=1,2,3,…f=\frac{nv}{2L},\qquad n=1,2,3,\dotsf=2Lnv​,n=1,2,3,…
  • Closed at one end: L=nλ4L=n\frac{\lambda}{4}L=n4λ​ with odd nnn only, f=nv4L,n=1,3,5,…f=\frac{nv}{4L},\qquad n=1,3,5,\dotsf=4Lnv​,n=1,3,5,… Its fundamental is half that of an open pipe of the same length.
  • Strings follow fn=nv2Lf_n=\frac{nv}{2L}fn​=2Lnv​ (Module 16-7). The mix of harmonics gives each instrument its own sound.
Worked example17-5

A pipe is 0.500.500.50 m long. Take v=340v=340v=340 m/s.

  1. (a)Find its two lowest resonant frequencies when it is open at both ends.
  2. (b)Find them when it is closed at one end.
  3. (c)How long is a pipe, closed at one end, whose fundamental is 858585 Hz?
Show solutionHide solution

17-6Beats

Class 45 · Fri 11 Dec

  • Two nearly equal frequencies heard together: the sound swells and fades as the waves drift in and out of step.
  • The beat frequency is their difference, the larger minus the smaller: fbeat=f1−f2f_\text{beat}=f_1-f_2fbeat​=f1​−f2​ The pitch heard is the average, f1+f22.\frac{f_1+f_2}{2}.2f1​+f2​​.
  • Tuning: the beats slow down and vanish as the two frequencies come together.
Worked example17-6

A 440440440 Hz tuning fork and a guitar string sound together with 333 beats per second.

  1. (a)What can the string's frequency be?
  2. (b)Tightening the string a little makes the beats faster. Which frequency was it?
  3. (c)What pitch is heard while the beats sound?
  4. (d)By roughly what percentage must the tension change to remove the beats?
Show solutionHide solution

17-7The Doppler effect

Class 46 · Mon 14 Dec

  • Motion changes the frequency heard. A source or a detector moving through the air changes the frequency detected, f′f'f′, from the emitted fff: f′=f v±vDv∓vSf'=f\,\frac{v\pm v_D}{v\mp v_S}f′=fv∓vS​v±vD​​ with vvv the speed of sound in the air.
  • The sign rule. Motion toward the other raises the frequency, motion away lowers it: choose the signs that do that. The detector's speed vDv_DvD​ goes on top, the source's vSv_SvS​ below.
  • Not symmetric. A moving source and a moving detector, at the same speed, give slightly different shifts.
Worked example17-7

A siren emits 990990990 Hz. Take v=340v=340v=340 m/s in still air.

  1. (a)The siren moves at 343434 m/s straight toward a listener at rest. What frequency is heard?
  2. (b)What is heard once it moves away at 343434 m/s?
  3. (c)The siren is at rest and the listener moves toward it at 343434 m/s. What is heard?
  4. (d)And when the listener moves away at 343434 m/s?
Show solutionHide solution

17-8Supersonic speeds, shock waves

Class 46 · Mon 14 Dec

  • Faster than sound (vS>vv_S>vvS​>v), the wavefronts pile up into a cone, the Mach cone, with half-angle θ\thetaθ: sin⁡θ=vvS\sin\theta=\frac{v}{v_S}sinθ=vS​v​
  • The Mach number is vSv\frac{v_S}{v}vvS​​.
  • A sonic boom is the cone's surface sweeping past a listener: a sudden jump in pressure.
Worked example17-8

A jet flies level at Mach 2.02.02.0, 5.05.05.0 km above the ground. Take v=340v=340v=340 m/s.

  1. (a)Find its speed.
  2. (b)Find the half-angle of its Mach cone.
  3. (c)How far past an observer on the ground (measured along the ground) is the jet when the observer hears the boom?
  4. (d)How long after the jet passed overhead is that?
Show solutionHide solution

Watch out

  • Doppler signs: decide first whether the frequency goes up (toward) or down (away), then pick the signs.
  • The vvv in the Doppler formula is the speed of sound, and every speed is measured relative to the air.
  • Decibels don't add: two equal sources give 333 dB more, not twice the level.
  • A pipe closed at one end has only the odd harmonics.
  • A path difference of λ2\frac{\lambda}{2}2λ​ cancels; one of λ\lambdaλ reinforces.
  • The intensity falls as 1r2\frac{1}{r^2}r21​, the amplitude only as 1r\frac{1}{r}r1​.

Chapter 18 · Modules 18-1 to 18-6 · 17–21 Dec

Temperature, heat and the first law of thermodynamics

18-1Temperature

Class 48 · Thu 17 Dec

  • Temperature is an SI base quantity, measured in kelvins (K). Nothing is colder than absolute zero, 000 K.
  • The zeroth law. If bodies A and B are each in thermal equilibrium with a third body T, they are in thermal equilibrium with each other. That is why a thermometer works.
  • The fixed point. The triple point of water, where ice, liquid water and vapour coexist, is T3=273.16T_3=273.16T3​=273.16 K.
  • The constant-volume gas thermometer reads the pressure of a gas held at a fixed volume: T=(273.16 K)lim⁡gas→0pp3T=(273.16\ \text{K})\lim_{\text{gas}\to0}\frac{p}{p_3}T=(273.16 K)gas→0lim​p3​p​

A constant-volume gas thermometer reads 50.050.050.0 kPa at the triple point of water. Treat its gas as ideal.

  2. (b)What would it read at 000 K?
  3. (c)What does it read at 546.32546.32546.32 K?

18-2The Celsius and Fahrenheit scales

Class 48 · Thu 17 Dec

  • Celsius is the Kelvin scale shifted: TC=T−273.15∘.T_C=T-273.15^\circ.TC​=T−273.15∘. A change of 1 ∘1\ ^\circ1 ∘C equals a change of 111 K.
  • Fahrenheit has smaller degrees: TF=95TC+32∘T_F=\tfrac{9}{5}T_C+32^\circTF​=59​TC​+32∘ A change of 1 ∘1\ ^\circ1 ∘C is a change of 1.8 ∘1.8\ ^\circ1.8 ∘F.
  • Fixed points: water freezes at 0 ∘0\ ^\circ0 ∘C =32 ∘=32\ ^\circ=32 ∘F and boils at 100 ∘100\ ^\circ100 ∘C =212 ∘=212\ ^\circ=212 ∘F; −40 ∘-40\ ^\circ−40 ∘C is also −40 ∘-40\ ^\circ−40 ∘F.

18-3Thermal expansion

Class 48 · Thu 17 Dec

  • Linear expansion. A rod of length LLL warmed by ΔT\Delta TΔT grows by ΔL=Lα ΔT\Delta L=L\alpha\,\Delta TΔL=LαΔT with α\alphaα, the coefficient of linear expansion, in K−1\text{K}^{-1}K−1 (the same as per ∘^\circ∘C).
  • Volume expansion: ΔV=Vβ ΔT,\Delta V=V\beta\,\Delta T,ΔV=VβΔT, with β=3α\beta=3\alphaβ=3α for a solid.
  • A hole expands too, as if it were filled with the material around it.
  • Water is odd: between 0 ∘0\ ^\circ0 ∘C and 4 ∘4\ ^\circ4 ∘C it shrinks as it warms, so it is densest at 4 ∘4\ ^\circ4 ∘C.

18-4Absorption of heat

Class 49 · Fri 18 Dec

  • Heat QQQ is energy that flows because of a temperature difference: into a system (Q>0Q>0Q>0) or out of it (Q<0Q<0Q<0). 1 cal=4.1861\text{ cal}=4.1861 cal=4.186 J.
  • Warming without a change of phase: Q=cm ΔTQ=cm\,\Delta TQ=cmΔT with the specific heat ccc; water has c=4186 J/(kg⋅K),c=4186\ \text{J/(kg}\cdot\text{K)},c=4186 J/(kg⋅K), which is 1 cal/(g⋅K).1\ \text{cal/(g}\cdot\text{K)}.1 cal/(g⋅K).
  • A change of phase happens at a fixed temperature and takes the heat of transformation LLL: Q=LmQ=LmQ=Lm For water LF=333L_F=333LF​=333 kJ/kg (melting) and LV=2256L_V=2256LV​=2256 kJ/kg (boiling).
  • Mixing in an insulated container: the heats add up to zero, ∑Q=0\sum Q=0∑Q=0.

18-5The first law of thermodynamics

Class 50 · Mon 21 Dec

  • Work done by a gas as its volume changes is the area under its path on a ppp-VVV diagram: W=∫ViVfp dVW=\int_{V_i}^{V_f}p\,dVW=∫Vi​Vf​​pdV It depends on the path, and so does the heat.
  • The first law. The internal energy changes by the heat added minus the work the gas does: ΔEint=Q−W\Delta E_\text{int}=Q-WΔEint​=Q−W
  • Special processes: adiabatic (Q=0Q=0Q=0), ΔEint=−W\Delta E_\text{int}=-WΔEint​=−W; constant volume (W=0W=0W=0), ΔEint=Q\Delta E_\text{int}=QΔEint​=Q; a closed cycle (ΔEint=0\Delta E_\text{int}=0ΔEint​=0), Q=WQ=WQ=W; free expansion (Q=W=0Q=W=0Q=W=0), ΔEint=0.\Delta E_\text{int}=0.ΔEint​=0.
  • At constant pressure W=p ΔVW=p\,\Delta VW=pΔV.

18-6Heat transfer mechanisms

Not on the class scheduleThe schedule doesn’t list it; it may come up in a class marked TBD.

  • Conduction through a slab of area AAA, thickness LLL and thermal conductivity kkk, between temperatures THT_HTH​ and TCT_CTC​: Pcond=kATH−TCLP_\text{cond}=kA\frac{T_H-T_C}{L}Pcond​=kALTH​−TC​​ Its thermal resistance is R=LkR=\frac{L}{k}R=kL​; slabs in series add their resistances.
  • Convection: a moving fluid carries the energy, like warm air rising from a heater.
  • Radiation: every body emits electromagnetic waves. With the Stefan–Boltzmann constant σ=5.67×10−8 W/(m2⋅K4)\sigma=5.67\times10^{-8}\ \text{W/(m}^2\text{}\cdot\text{K}^4\text{)}σ=5.67×10−8 W/(m2⋅K4) and the emissivity ε\varepsilonε (111 for a blackbody): Prad=σεAT4P_\text{rad}=\sigma\varepsilon AT^4Prad​=σεAT4 with TTT in kelvins. Twice the temperature gives sixteen times the power.

Watch out

  • Using ∘^\circ∘C where kelvins are needed: ratios, pV=nRTpV=nRTpV=nRT and T4T^4T4. A temperature difference is the same in both.
  • The sign of WWW: positive when the gas expands and does work.
  • QQQ and WWW depend on the path; ΔEint\Delta E_\text{int}ΔEint​ doesn't.
  • During melting or boiling the temperature stays fixed: use Q=LmQ=LmQ=Lm, not cmΔTcm\Delta TcmΔT.
  • Mixing: write each Q=cm(Tf−Ti)Q=cm(T_f-T_i)Q=cm(Tf​−Ti​) with its own sign and set the sum to zero.

Not on the class scheduleThe schedule doesn’t list it; it may come up in a class marked TBD.

  • Adiabatic means no heat flows, Q=0Q=0Q=0, as in a fast or well-insulated process. For a slow (quasi-static) one, pVγ=constant,TVγ−1=constantpV^\gamma=\text{constant},\qquad TV^{\gamma-1}=\text{constant}pVγ=constant,TVγ−1=constant
  • The work comes out of the internal energy, W=−ΔEint=nCV(Ti−Tf)W=-\Delta E_\text{int}=nC_V(T_i-T_f)W=−ΔEint​=nCV​(Ti​−Tf​): an expanding gas cools, and a compressed one heats up (the diesel engine).
  • Free expansion into a vacuum is different: Q=W=0Q=W=0Q=W=0, so an ideal gas keeps its temperature, and pVγpV^\gammapVγ doesn't apply.
Worked example19-9

1.01.01.0 mol of a monatomic ideal gas (γ=53\displaystyle \gamma=\frac{5}{3}γ=35​) at 400400400 K expands slowly and adiabatically to 888 times its volume. Use R=8.31 J/(mol⋅K).R=8.31\ \text{J/(mol}\cdot\text{K)}.R=8.31 J/(mol⋅K).

  1. (a)Find the final temperature.
  2. (b)By what factor does the pressure fall?
  3. (c)Find the work done by the gas.
Show solutionHide solution

Watch out

  • Temperatures in kelvins, molar masses in kg/mol: 282828 g/mol is 0.0280.0280.028 kg/mol.
  • RRR is per mole, kkk per molecule: pV=nRT=NkTpV=nRT=NkTpV=nRT=NkT.
  • CVC_VCV​ belongs to constant volume; at constant pressure use Cp=CV+RC_p=C_V+RCp​=CV​+R.
  • Adiabatic isn't isothermal: pVγpV^\gammapVγ, not pVpVpV, stays the same.
  • A free expansion has Q=0Q=0Q=0 but isn't the slow adiabatic process: its temperature doesn't change.

Chapter 20 · Modules 20-1 to 20-4 · 8–15 Jan

Entropy and the second law of thermodynamics

20-1Entropy

Class 57 · Fri 8 Jan

  • One-way processes. Heat flows from hot to cold, and a gas spreads through a box; these irreversible processes never run backward by themselves. Entropy SSS tells their direction.
  • The change in entropy between two states, along any reversible path between them: ΔS=∫ifdQT\Delta S=\int_i^f\frac{dQ}{T}ΔS=∫if​TdQ​ At a constant temperature, ΔS=QT.\Delta S=\frac{Q}{T}.ΔS=TQ​. Entropy is a state function: ΔS\Delta SΔS depends only on the two states.
  • The second law. In a closed system, entropy increases in an irreversible process and stays the same in a reversible one; it never decreases: ΔS≥0\Delta S\ge0ΔS≥0.
  • An ideal gas, from (Vi,Ti)(V_i,T_i)(Vi​,Ti​) to (Vf,Tf)(V_f,T_f)(Vf​,Tf​) by any process: ΔS=nRln⁡VfVi+nCVln⁡TfTi\Delta S=nR\ln\frac{V_f}{V_i}+nC_V\ln\frac{T_f}{T_i}ΔS=nRlnVi​Vf​​+nCV​lnTi​Tf​​
Worked example20-1

Use R=8.31 J/(mol⋅K),R=8.31\ \text{J/(mol}\cdot\text{K)},R=8.31 J/(mol⋅K), ln⁡2≈0.693\ln2\approx0.693ln2≈0.693, and LF=333L_F=333LF​=333 kJ/kg for ice.

  1. (a)1.01.01.0 mol of an ideal gas doubles its volume at a constant 300300300 K. Find its change in entropy.
  2. (b)The same gas doubles its volume by a free expansion into a vacuum. Find its change in entropy.
  3. (c)Find the change in entropy of 1.01.01.0 kg of ice as it melts at 273273273 K.

20-2Entropy in the real world: engines

Class 58 · Tue 12 Jan

  • A heat engine takes heat ∣QH∣|Q_H|∣QH​∣ from a hot reservoir, does work ∣W∣|W|∣W∣, and gives heat ∣QL∣|Q_L|∣QL​∣ to a cold one. Over a cycle ∣W∣=∣QH∣−∣QL∣|W|=|Q_H|-|Q_L|∣W∣=∣QH​∣−∣QL​∣
  • Efficiency is what you get over what you pay for: ε=∣W∣∣QH∣\varepsilon=\frac{|W|}{|Q_H|}ε=∣QH​∣∣W∣​
  • The Carnot engine, the ideal reversible engine, has ∣QH∣TH=∣QL∣TL\frac{|Q_H|}{T_H}=\frac{|Q_L|}{T_L}TH​∣QH​∣​=TL​∣QL​∣​ and εC=1−TLTH\varepsilon_C=1-\frac{T_L}{T_H}εC​=1−TH​TL​​ No engine working between the same two temperatures does better.
  • No perfect engine: ε<1\varepsilon<1ε<1; some heat must always go to the cold reservoir (the second law).
Worked example20-2

A Carnot engine works between 600600600 K and 300300300 K and takes in 120012001200 J of heat each cycle.

  1. (a)Find its efficiency.
  2. (b)Find the work it does each cycle.
  3. (c)How much heat goes to the cold reservoir each cycle?
  4. (d)An inventor claims an engine between the same reservoirs that does 700700700 J of work from 120012001200 J of heat. Can it work?

20-3Refrigerators and real engines

Not on the class scheduleThe schedule doesn’t list it; it may come up in a class marked TBD.

  • A refrigerator uses work ∣W∣|W|∣W∣ to move heat ∣QL∣|Q_L|∣QL​∣ from a cold reservoir to a hot one, which receives ∣QH∣=∣QL∣+∣W∣|Q_H|=|Q_L|+|W|∣QH​∣=∣QL​∣+∣W∣
  • The coefficient of performance, what you get over what you pay for: K=∣QL∣∣W∣,KC=TLTH−TL (Carnot)K=\frac{|Q_L|}{|W|},\qquad K_C=\frac{T_L}{T_H-T_L}\ \text{(Carnot)}K=∣W∣∣QL​∣​,KC​=TH​−TL​TL​​ (Carnot)
  • No perfect refrigerator: heat never flows from cold to hot without work. Real engines and refrigerators do worse than Carnot ones.
Worked example20-3

A Carnot refrigerator keeps its inside at 270270270 K in a room at 300300300 K.

  1. (a)Find its coefficient of performance.
  2. (b)How much work does it need to remove 900900900 J of heat from the inside?
  3. (c)How much heat does the room receive then?

20-4A statistical view of entropy

Class 59 · Fri 15 Jan

  • Configurations and microstates. With NNN molecules in a box with two halves, a configuration says how many are in each half; a microstate says which ones. A configuration with n1n_1n1​ on one side and n2n_2n2​ on the other has the multiplicity W=N!n1! n2!W=\frac{N!}{n_1!\,n_2!}W=n1​!n2​!N!​
  • Equally likely microstates. Every microstate is as likely as any other, so the configuration with the largest WWW, the even split, is the most probable. For large NNN nearly all microstates are close to it.
  • Boltzmann's entropy equation: S=kln⁡WS=k\ln WS=klnW
Worked example20-4

Four identical molecules move about in a box with two halves. Use k=1.38×10−23k=1.38\times10^{-23}k=1.38×10−23 J/K and ln⁡6≈1.79\ln6\approx1.79ln6≈1.79.

  1. (a)Find the multiplicity of the configuration with two molecules in each half.
  2. (b)How many microstates are there in all? What is the chance of finding all four in the left half?
  3. (c)Find the difference in entropy between the two-two configuration and the four-zero one.
Show solutionHide solution

Watch out

  • ΔS=QT\Delta S=\frac{Q}{T}ΔS=TQ​ holds for a reversible process at constant TTT. For anything else, choose a reversible path between the same two states.
  • Kelvins in εC=1−TLTH\varepsilon_C=1-\frac{T_L}{T_H}εC​=1−TH​TL​​ and in KCK_CKC​, never ∘^\circ∘C.
  • Efficiency is ∣W∣∣QH∣,\frac{|W|}{|Q_H|},∣QH​∣∣W∣​, not ∣W∣∣QL∣.\frac{|W|}{|Q_L|}.∣QL​∣∣W∣​.
  • A system's entropy can fall if its surroundings' rises more; the total for a closed system never decreases.
  • A free expansion has Q=0Q=0Q=0 but ΔS>0\Delta S>0ΔS>0.

Exam-day habits

  • Kelvins. Turn temperatures into kelvins for ratios, pV=nRTpV=nRTpV=nRT, T4T^4T4, entropy and efficiency; a temperature difference can stay in ∘^\circ∘C.
  • Radians. Phases in SHM and waves, ωt+ϕ\omega t+\phiωt+ϕ and kx−ωtkx-\omega tkx−ωt, are in radians.
  • Read the wave first. From y=ymsin⁡(kx−ωt)y=y_m\sin(kx-\omega t)y=ym​sin(kx−ωt) write down ymy_mym​, kkk and ω\omegaω, then λ=2πk,\lambda=\frac{2\pi}{k},λ=k2π​, f=ω2πf=\frac{\omega}{2\pi}f=2πω​ and v=ωk.v=\frac{\omega}{k}.v=kω​.
  • Signs before numbers. Heat into the gas is positive, and so is work by an expanding gas; for a Doppler shift, decide up or down first.
  • No calculator. Keep π\piπ, 2\sqrt22​ and ln⁡2\ln2ln2 as they are, use log⁡2≈0.30\log2\approx0.30log2≈0.30 and ln⁡2≈0.69\ln2\approx0.69ln2≈0.69, and round only the final answer.
  • Check a special case. No damping, a source at rest, equal temperatures: the answer should turn into one you already know.
